sentences.text: Dromornis species were flightless birds with greatly reduced wings and large legs, resembling modern ostriches or emus.
The name Dromornis is derived from Ancient Greek words meaning 'course' or 'race' and 'bird'.
Eggs of Dromornis are estimated to be 30–34 cm long, 24–29 cm wide, and weigh 12.6–14.7 kg, making them among the largest known bird eggs.
The genus Dromornis was described by Richard Owen in 1872.
The type specimen of Dromornis australis was a femur found in a 55-meter well at Peak Downs, Queensland, and described by Owen in 1872.
Dromornis murrayi was described in 2016 based on fossils found among the Riversleigh fauna in Queensland, Australia.
Dromornis species were likely predominantly or exclusively herbivorous browsers.
While some researchers considered Dromornis planei carnivorous due to its large shearing beak, most currently agree it was a herbivore.
Gastroliths found with Dromornis planei suggest a herbivorous diet, though some suggestions propose it had carnivorous abilities similar to terror birds.
Dromornis stirtoni likely existed alongside other dromornithids and browsing marsupials as an apex herbivore.
The type species of the genus Dromornis is Dromornis australis.
Dromornis belongs to the family Dromornithidae, which includes extinct flightless birds known as mihirungs.
The term 'mihirung paringmal' is an Aboriginal word from the Tjapwuring people meaning 'giant bird'.
Although resembling giant emus, Dromornis is more closely related to early waterfowl of the Anseriformes order or a basal galliform.
In 2010, Nguyen and Boles suggested that Bullockornis is a species of Dromornis based on skeletal traits and phylogenetic analyses, a view supported by subsequent studies.
Dromornis species lived in Australia from the Oligocene to the Pliocene epochs.
Fossils of Dromornis australis are found in Pliocene deposits in Australia.
Dromornis murrayi lived during the Oligocene to early Miocene and is the earliest known species of the genus.
Fossils of Dromornis murrayi at the Riversleigh Hiatus site date to the early Miocene and the late Oligocene to early Miocene.
It is debated whether Dromornis planei is related to geese and ducks or to Galliformes, with some studies supporting the latter.
There is a debate regarding diet, but it is widely accepted that Dromornis stirtoni was mostly herbivorous, possibly occasionally scavenging or eating smaller prey.
Various factors are proposed to have contributed to the extinction of Dromornis stirtoni.
Murray and Vickers-Rich suggested Dromornis stirtoni went extinct because it was out-competed for food sources due to dietary overlap with other large animals.
